What are good free physiotherapy exercises for arthritis at home?

Note

NICE NG226 recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to you, such as local muscle strengthening and aerobic fitness, as a core osteoarthritis treatment. The NHS advises regular low-impact activity like walking, swimming or yoga. Start gently, keep effort around 4 out of 10, and build up slowly; next-day soreness means do less, not stop.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

Frequently asked questions

Living with arthritis can make movement feel scary. These routines are gentle on purpose — free, plain-English, and designed so you can take one small step today without a gym or a lecture.

Exercise is one of the main treatments for osteoarthritis, and NICE recommends strengthening and general fitness exercise as core care. Start today with a few gentle movements, keep the effort comfortable, and build up slowly. Some aching while you exercise is normal; if pain is much worse the next day, do a bit less next time rather than stopping. Motion is lotion.

What are the best exercises for arthritis?

Note

A mix usually works best: low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming, strengthening exercises for the muscles around painful joints, and gentle movement for flexibility and balance such as tai chi or yoga. NICE recommends therapeutic exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis, and UK guidance for adults is to build towards 150 minutes of moderate activity a week with strengthening on at least two days. The best exercise is one you can keep doing.

Exercise today: start here

  1. Check the red flags in the box below. If any apply, get help before you exercise.
  2. Warm up for a few minutes: march on the spot, roll your shoulders or circle your ankles.
  3. Pick one routine for the joint that bothers you most: knee, hip, , or .
  4. Do a few slow repetitions at a comfortable effort. You should be able to talk while you move.
  5. Check how you feel tomorrow and adjust using the pain guide below. Little and often beats one big session.

In pain right now? Start with the pain relief guide, then come back to gentle movement.

Red flags: stop and get help

Do not exercise the joint, and call NHS 111 or your GP for a same-day appointment if:

  • one joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever or feeling unwell
  • you take medicines that lower your immunity, such as methotrexate or biologics, and you have signs of infection
  • a joint is very painful after a fall or injury, or you cannot put weight on a leg

Stop and call 999 if you get chest pain or tightness, severe breathlessness, or feel faint while exercising.

Is it safe? How to read pain when you exercise

Exercise is unlikely to harm your joints. NICE advises explaining this to people with osteoarthritis, along with the fact that some extra aching at first can happen.

  • Mild ache that settles within a day: usually fine. Carry on and build up slowly.
  • Pain much worse the next day, or more swelling: do fewer repetitions or a shorter session next time. Do not stop altogether.
  • Sharp, catching pain, or a joint that gives way: stop that exercise and ask a physiotherapist.

Worried exercise will make things worse? Read can exercise make osteoarthritis worse?

Pick your starting point

  • Newly diagnosed: start with the newly diagnosed guide, then one routine from this page.
  • Knee or hip osteoarthritis: the knee routine, the hip routine and walking with arthritis.
  • Rheumatoid or other inflammatory arthritis: NICE says you should be able to see a specialist physiotherapist. Keep to gentle movement in a flare and follow your rheumatology team. See rheumatoid arthritis and chair-based exercise for RA.
  • Unsteady, older or low on energy: start seated with seated strength and sit-to-stand practice; after a fall, see confidence after a fall.
  • Joint replacement or recent surgery: follow the exercises your surgical or physiotherapy team gave you before using general routines.
  • Pool or water: swimming for hip osteoarthritis; the water supports your weight.

Flare days: do less, not nothing

  • Swap strengthening for gentle range-of-movement: bend and straighten the joint slowly a few times every hour.
  • Cut the time or repetitions, rather than stopping. Complete rest makes stiffness worse.
  • Use heat on stiff joints, or a wrapped cold pack on a hot, swollen joint, for up to about 20 minutes.
  • Build back up over a few days once the flare settles. Use the flare-up guide and the printable flare action plan.

When to see your GP or a physiotherapist

  • pain or swelling keeps getting worse after exercise, even when you do less
  • you are not sure which exercises are safe after an injury, an operation or a joint replacement
  • you have heart or lung problems, or feel dizzy or breathless with gentle activity
  • a joint locks, gives way or you are falling

In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy without seeing a GP: check your GP surgery or local NHS website. Waiting already? See help while you are on a waiting list.

Quick Exercise Tips

Simple guidelines for safe, effective arthritis exercise.

Warm Up

Five minutes of gentle marching or shoulder rolls before you load a sore joint.

Good Shoes

Cushioned, supportive footwear makes walking easier on knees and hips.

Pace Yourself

Keep effort around 4 out of 10. Next-day soreness means do less, not more.

Ice After

Ten minutes of ice on a warm, swollen joint, cloth barrier, after you finish.

Be Consistent

A short daily session beats one long weekend burst that leaves you sore.

Listen to Pain

Sharp or worsening pain means stop. A mild ache that settles is usually fine.

Chair-based movement for older adults

As the UK population ages, maintaining mobility and independence becomes a paramount concern for older adults and the people supporting them. Exercise is often called the closest thing we have to a “magic pill” for healthy ageing — but for many people living with arthritis, traditional high-impact workouts are not realistic because of joint degeneration, balance issues or chronic pain. This is where low-impact movement, and chair exercises in particular, become genuinely useful. Short, accessible routines — often as little as ten minutes a day — meet people where they are and remove the intimidation of a long gym session.

Chair exercises address several of the physiological changes that come with ageing. First, they reduce the risk of falls and injury by giving people a stable base while they work. By staying seated, you can focus on the muscular action without the cognitive load of worrying about balance. Second, they are good for the heart. You do not need to run a marathon to elevate your heart rate. Arm circles, seated marching, torso twists and gentle boxing motions, performed in sequence, raise circulation, help manage blood pressure and support long-term cardiovascular health.

The benefits extend well beyond the physical. Regular activity releases endorphins, the body’s natural mood lifters, which can help offset the isolation, anxiety or low mood that sometimes accompany later life. Light resistance work using small hand weights or resistance bands during a chair workout pushes back against sarcopenia — the age-related loss of muscle mass. Preserved muscle strength is what allows older adults to keep doing the Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) that protect autonomy: cooking, washing, dressing, getting on and off the toilet, and managing stairs.

For people living specifically with arthritis, gentle movement keeps the joints lubricated and the surrounding tissues flexible, which reduces the morning stiffness that often triggers further inactivity and pain. The key is consistency rather than intensity. A short daily routine is far more useful than a punishing weekly session that leaves you sore for days. Build the habit first, then add reps, light resistance or a few extra minutes as you adapt. Proper form matters more than effort — slow, controlled movement is what protects joints and tendons.

This is general information, not medical advice. Speak to a GP, physiotherapist or rheumatologist before starting any new exercise programme, especially if you have heart, balance or joint conditions.

For carers and family

Encourage little and often rather than doing everything for the person. Stand nearby for balance work, use a sturdy chair without wheels, and keep a note of what they managed so you can both see progress. Stop and get help if they become breathless, dizzy or have chest pain, or if a joint becomes hot, red and swollen. Looking after someone? You may be entitled to a carer's assessment.

Pillar Guide

Evidence-based anti-inflammatory and Mediterranean eating for arthritis in the UK — what helps, what to limit, omega-3s, supplements and a practical meal plan.

Best arthritis diet advice UK: an anti-inflammatory Mediterranean pattern — vegetables, oily fish, olive oil, wholegrains and pulses — is the best-evidenced approach. It may support joint comfort for some people but does not replace prescribed treatment.

What is the best diet for arthritis?

Note

The NHS advises a healthy, balanced diet and keeping to a healthy weight, because extra weight strains your joints. NICE NG226 says any weight loss helps people with osteoarthritis who are overweight, and NG100 encourages people with rheumatoid arthritis to follow Mediterranean principles: more fruit, vegetables, fish and plant oils, less meat.

Key clinical takeaways

  • No diet cures arthritis; a balanced diet supports exercise, medicines and your other treatment.
  • If you have osteoarthritis and are overweight, any weight loss helps, and losing 10% of body weight is likely better than 5% (NICE NG226).
  • NICE NG100 encourages Mediterranean diet principles for rheumatoid arthritis: more fruit, vegetables, fish and plant oils, less meat.
  • Don't drink too much alcohol, and follow your rheumatology team's limits if you take methotrexate.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best diet for arthritis joint pain?

Note

The best diet for arthritis is the Mediterranean diet — rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, olive oil, oily fish, nuts and pulses. NHS and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) guidance supports a Mediterranean-style pattern for general health and joint-friendly eating. For osteoarthritis, gradual weight loss where appropriate (often discussed as around 5–10% of body weight with a clinician) can ease load on weight-bearing joints — this is educational, not a personal target.

Why Diet Matters for Arthritis

The relationship between diet and arthritis is one of the most researched areas in rheumatology. While no single food can cure arthritis, mounting evidence demonstrates that what you eat can significantly influence inflammation levels, pain intensity, joint stiffness, disease activity and even the effectiveness of medications. Reviews of Mediterranean-style and anti-inflammatory dietary patterns (including work summarised for clinicians in journals such as Nutrients) suggest diet can support lower pain and inflammatory markers for some people — effects vary, and diet does not replace prescribed treatment.

For people with osteoarthritis, diet also plays a critical role in weight management. Excess weight is the single most modifiable risk factor for OA: every 1 kg of body weight lost reduces the load on each knee by approximately 4 kg with every step (Messier et al., 2013). For overweight individuals with knee OA, losing just 5–10% of body weight can produce clinically meaningful reductions in pain and improvements in function.

The Mediterranean Diet: The Gold Standard

The Mediterranean diet is the most extensively studied dietary pattern for arthritis and chronic inflammation. It consistently outperforms other diets in clinical trials for reducing inflammatory markers, joint pain and cardiovascular risk — which is elevated in people with inflammatory arthritis.

Want a plan to follow this week? See the focused 7-day Mediterranean eating plan for arthritis — UK shopping list, recipes and what to eat freely, weekly and rarely.

Core Principles

  • Abundant vegetables and fruits — aim for 7+ portions daily, focusing on colourful varieties rich in antioxidants (berries, leafy greens, tomatoes, peppers, beetroot)
  • Wholegrains — oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread, quinoa, bulgur wheat
  • Healthy fats — extra virgin olive oil as the primary fat source (rich in oleocanthal, which has ibuprofen-like anti-inflammatory properties)
  • Oily fish — at least 2 portions per week (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout) for omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA
  • Legumes and pulses — lentils, chickpeas, beans — excellent protein and fibre sources
  • Nuts and seeds — walnuts (highest plant omega-3), almonds, flaxseeds, chia seeds
  • Herbs and spices — turmeric, ginger, garlic, oregano, rosemary — many have documented anti-inflammatory properties
  • Moderate dairy — yoghurt and cheese in moderation; fermented dairy supports gut health
  • Limited red meat — no more than 1–2 portions per week; processed meats avoided
  • Limited sugar and refined carbohydrates — these promote inflammation

A landmark 2023 trial in Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases found that RA patients following a Mediterranean diet for 16 weeks experienced a significant reduction in DAS28 scores (a composite measure of disease activity) compared to controls, with improvements in fatigue and quality of life.

Key Anti-Inflammatory Foods

Omega-3 Fatty Acids

Omega-3s are the most well-evidenced dietary component for arthritis. EPA and DHA — found primarily in oily fish — are converted into anti-inflammatory compounds called resolvins and protectins that actively help resolve inflammation. A 2017 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology found that fish oil supplementation (2–4 g/day of combined EPA/DHA) significantly reduced joint pain, morning stiffness and NSAID use in RA patients.

Best food sources:

  • Salmon (wild-caught) — 2.2 g omega-3 per 100 g
  • Mackerel — 2.6 g per 100 g
  • Sardines — 1.5 g per 100 g
  • Trout — 1.0 g per 100 g
  • Walnuts — 2.5 g ALA (plant omega-3) per 30 g
  • Flaxseeds — 6.7 g ALA per 30 g (ground for absorption)
  • Chia seeds — 5.0 g ALA per 30 g

Recommendation: Aim for 2 portions of oily fish per week plus daily plant sources. If you don't eat fish, consider an algae-based omega-3 supplement (providing EPA/DHA directly).

Turmeric and Curcumin

Turmeric's active compound, curcumin, is one of the most extensively studied natural anti-inflammatory agents. It works by blocking NF-ÎºB — a master regulator of inflammation — and inhibiting COX-2 and LOX enzymes (similar mechanisms to NSAIDs like ibuprofen). A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Medicinal Food concluded that 1,000 mg/day of curcumin significantly reduced pain and improved function in knee OA patients.

Key considerations:

  • Curcumin has poor bioavailability on its own — pairing with black pepper (piperine) increases absorption by up to 2,000%
  • Study curcumin products differ from cooking turmeric — ask a clinician or pharmacist before using concentrated supplements
  • Some trials show curcumin provides comparable pain relief to diclofenac with fewer side effects
  • Consult your doctor if taking blood thinners or diabetes medication, as curcumin may interact

Ginger

Ginger contains gingerols and shogaols — bioactive compounds with anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties. A 2015 meta-analysis of 5 randomised controlled trials found that ginger supplementation (500–1,000 mg/day) significantly reduced OA pain compared to placebo. Fresh ginger can be used in cooking (1–2 cm fresh root daily) or as a tea.

Berries and Antioxidant-Rich Foods

Berries — particularly blueberries, strawberries, cherries and blackcurrants — are rich in anthocyanins, powerful antioxidants that reduce oxidative stress and inflammation. Tart cherry juice has been specifically studied for gout, where it has been shown to reduce uric acid levels and flare frequency. Other antioxidant-rich foods include dark leafy greens (kale, spinach), beetroot, sweet potatoes and dark chocolate (70%+ cocoa).

Foods That May Worsen Arthritis

While individual responses vary, certain foods are consistently associated with increased inflammation and worsened arthritis symptoms:

  • Processed and ultra-processed foods — ready meals, crisps, biscuits, processed meats (bacon, sausages, ham) — high in advanced glycation end products (AGEs) that promote inflammation
  • Added sugars — fizzy drinks, sweets, cakes — trigger inflammatory cytokine release
  • Refined carbohydrates — white bread, white pasta, pastries — spike blood sugar and insulin, promoting inflammation
  • Excessive alcohol — increases uric acid (worsens gout) and systemic inflammation
  • Excessive omega-6 fatty acids — found in sunflower oil, corn oil and many processed foods — when consumed in excess relative to omega-3, these promote pro-inflammatory pathways
  • Trans fats — hydrogenated oils found in some margarines and commercial baked goods
  • Excessive red meat — particularly processed meats, which contain nitrites and saturated fats

Supplements: What the Evidence Says

Glucosamine and Chondroitin

These are the most widely used OA supplements in the UK. Evidence is mixed: a 2018 Cochrane review found glucosamine provides small, uncertain benefits for pain compared to placebo. Chondroitin alone showed similarly modest effects. Combined glucosamine/chondroitin may offer slightly better outcomes, but the evidence is not strong enough for NICE to recommend routine use.

Collagen (Hydrolysed)

Emerging research suggests hydrolysed collagen peptides (10 g/day) may modestly reduce joint pain and stiffness in OA. A 2019 meta-analysis in International Orthopaedics found statistically significant improvements in pain and function, though effect sizes were small. Collagen is generally well-tolerated.

Vitamin D

Vitamin D deficiency is extremely common in the UK (affecting up to 1 in 5 adults) and is associated with worse arthritis outcomes. The health service recommends all UK adults take a 10 mcg (400 IU) vitamin D supplement daily during autumn and winter. People with inflammatory arthritis may benefit from higher doses (discuss with your doctor).

Fish Oil (Omega-3 Supplements)

If you don't consume enough oily fish, a high-quality fish oil supplement providing 1–3 g of combined EPA/DHA daily is the most well-evidenced supplement for arthritis. Look for purified, sustainably sourced products with high EPA content. Algae-based alternatives are equally effective for vegetarians and vegans.

Gut Health and Arthritis

Emerging research links the gut microbiome to inflammatory arthritis. An imbalanced gut microbiome (dysbiosis) may trigger or worsen autoimmune responses in conditions like RA and PsA. To support gut health:

  • Eat 30+ different plant foods per week — diversity feeds diverse beneficial bacteria
  • Include fermented foods — kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, live yoghurt, miso
  • Consume prebiotic fibre — garlic, onions, leeks, asparagus, bananas, oats
  • Limit artificial sweeteners and emulsifiers — these may disrupt gut bacteria

Weight Management for Joint Health

Maintaining a healthy weight is arguably the most impactful dietary intervention for OA. Evidence-based strategies include:

  • Focus on nutrient-dense, high-satiety foods — vegetables, protein, wholegrains and healthy fats keep you fuller for longer
  • Avoid crash diets — they lead to muscle loss, which worsens joint instability
  • Aim for gradual weight loss — 0.5–1 kg per week is sustainable and preserves muscle mass
  • Combine dietary changes with regular low-impact exercise — walking, swimming, cycling
  • Consider portion control rather than food restriction — using smaller plates and mindful eating techniques

The NICE guidelines for OA (NG226) specifically recommend weight loss as a first-line treatment alongside exercise, stating it should be offered before medication.

Practical Tips for UK Shoppers

  • Budget-friendly options — tinned fish (sardines, mackerel), frozen berries, dried lentils and tinned chickpeas are just as nutritious as fresh alternatives
  • Read labels — look for traffic-light labels; aim for green on fat, sugar and salt
  • Buy seasonal UK produce — cheaper and more nutritious; farmer's markets often have better value
  • Batch cooking — prepare soups, stews and curries in bulk and freeze portions
  • Joint-friendly cooking — use electric can openers, lightweight pans and adaptive kitchen utensils from organisations like the Arthritis Action or OT referral

Anti-Inflammatory Smoothie Recipe

Beet & Berry Anti-Inflammatory Smoothie (serves 1):

  • 1 small cooked beetroot (peeled, chopped)
  • 1 cup frozen mixed berries
  • 1 banana
  • 1-inch fresh ginger (grated)
  • 1 tbsp ground flaxseed
  • 1 cup unsweetened almond milk or oat milk
  • Optional: 1 tsp turmeric powder + pinch black pepper

Blend until smooth. This provides omega-3 (flaxseed), betalains (beetroot), anthocyanins (berries), gingerols (ginger) and curcumin (turmeric) — a powerhouse of anti-inflammatory compounds in one glass.

CarbohydratesWholegrains and oatsWhite bread, pastries and sugary cereals
DrinksWater and unsweetened teaSugary drinks and too much alcohol

Nutrition quick tips

  • Eat oily fish: the NHS recommends at least 2 portions of fish a week, one of them oily, such as salmon, mackerel or sardines. Tinned fish counts.
  • Use olive oil: choose olive or other plant oils instead of butter where you can.
  • Add fruit: frozen supermarket berries count towards your 5 A Day.
  • Go green: add a portion of vegetables, such as frozen spinach, to one meal today.
  • Cook with spices: turmeric or ginger can flavour food. Supplements are optional and are not a cure.
  • Drink well: water or unsweetened tea instead of sugary drinks.

Diet for specific types of arthritis

Read the condition guides for advice that applies to your type of arthritis: osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout and lupus. For meal ideas, see the 7-day Mediterranean plan and foods to limit. For supplements, see the supplements hub.

Speak to your GP, pharmacist or a registered dietitian before changing your diet if you have other health conditions, take regular medicines, or plan to cut out whole food groups.

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide is based on evidence from NICE guidelines (NG226), systematic reviews published in Nutrients, Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases, British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, Journal of Medicinal Food, and guidance from the British Dietetic Association. Statistics cited are from the most recent publications available as of 2024. This information is for educational purposes only. Always consult a registered dietitian or your GP before making significant dietary changes, especially if you take medication.

/conditions/foot-and-ankle-arthritis:
Common types of foot and ankle arthritis

  • Big toe arthritis (hallux rigidus) — the most common foot osteoarthritis. The big toe stiffens and hurts when you push off; a bony bump often appears on top of the joint.
  • Midfoot arthritis — deep ache across the top of the foot, worse on uneven ground or after previous injury.
  • Ankle osteoarthritis — less common than knee or hip OA but often disabling; many cases follow an old fracture, dislocation or repeated severe sprain.
  • Rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis in the feet — small toe joints, ball-of-foot pain, swelling and deformity; footwear and early rheumatology care matter.

Gout also loves the big toe — see our gout guide if flares are sudden, hot and intensely painful.

What are the symptoms?

  • Pain with every step — or a deep ache that builds after walking
  • Morning stiffness — brief in osteoarthritis, often longer in inflammatory arthritis
  • Swelling — around the ankle, midfoot or big toe joint
  • Reduced push-off — especially with hallux rigidus
  • Instability or fear of falling — stiff, painful ankles alter balance (see our falls prevention guide)
  • Shoe struggle — standard footwear presses on bony bumps or swollen toes

What causes it?

  • Previous injury — ankle fractures and severe sprains are the leading risk for ankle OA
  • Age and cumulative load — cartilage wear in the big toe and midfoot after 50
  • Inflammatory disease — rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis frequently involve the feet
  • Biomechanics and footwear — high heels, narrow toe boxes and uncorrected flat or high-arch patterns
  • Family history — especially for hallux rigidus and Heberden-like patterns in the toes

Daily tasks most affected

Walking on uneven ground84% Standing for long periods78% Finding comfortable shoes72% Climbing stairs61% Getting going after sitting55%

What are the best exercises?

Keep the ankle and toes moving within a comfortable range. Warm the foot in a basin of warm water for 10 minutes first. Full routine: foot and ankle arthritis exercises.

Range of motion

  • Ankle circles — 10 each way, both feet
  • Alphabet tracing — write letters in the air with your big toe
  • Toe spreads and towel scrunches — strengthen intrinsic foot muscles

Strength and balance

  • Heel raises — hold a counter, rise onto toes, lower slowly. Build to 2 sets of 10–15
  • Band dorsiflexion — pull toes toward you against a light band
  • Single-leg stance — near a wall; progress toward 30 seconds each side

Avoid: high-impact jumping, barefoot walking on hard floors during flares, and forcing a painful big toe into deep bend.

Footwear, orthotics and lifestyle

  • Wide, deep toe box and adjustable fastenings for day-to-day swelling
  • Rocker or stiff sole for big toe arthritis to reduce joint bend at push-off
  • Removable insoles so NHS or private orthotics can fit
  • Low heel — under about 2.5 cm reduces forefoot pressure
  • Pair footwear changes with the same anti-inflammatory pattern in our Diet Hub

Daily foot-care checklist

Footwear

Wide toe box, grip sole, low heel.

Mobility

Ankle circles and toe work daily.

Balance

Brief single-leg practice near a counter.

Warm-up

Warm soak before the first walk.

How is it treated in the UK?

Self-management

  • Supportive shoes and activity pacing
  • Daily mobility and balance routine
  • Topical NSAID gel around the painful joint if suitable for you
  • Heat before activity; short ice packs after a flare

NHS pathway

  • GP — assessment, X-rays or blood tests when inflammatory disease is possible
  • Podiatry — biomechanics, orthotics, footwear advice
  • Physiotherapy — graded loading and balance (self-referral in many areas)
  • Orthopaedics — injections, fusion or replacement when conservative care is not enough
  • Rheumatology — if RA, PsA or other inflammatory disease is suspected

If referrals are delayed, our waiting-list help guide covers what you can do meanwhile.

When should you see your GP?

  • Foot or ankle pain lasting more than a few weeks
  • Warm, red or markedly swollen joint
  • New deformity, ulcers, or numbness in people with diabetes
  • Falls or near-falls linked to unstable ankles
  • Known inflammatory arthritis with a new foot flare

Frequently asked questions

What are the first signs of foot or ankle arthritis? Early signs include morning stiffness in the ankle or big toe, a deep ache with the first steps of the day, swelling around the joint after walking, and shoes that suddenly feel tight over a bony bump on top of the big toe joint. What is the best footwear for foot arthritis? Look for a wide, deep toe box, a firm heel counter, cushioned sole, low heel (under 2.5 cm) and adjustable fastenings. For big toe arthritis, a stiff or rocker sole reduces bending at the painful joint. Removable insoles leave room for orthotics. What exercises help ankle arthritis? Daily ankle circles, alphabet tracing with the big toe, towel scrunches, gentle calf raises and single-leg balance near a counter maintain mobility and stability. Stop short of sharp pain and warm the foot first. See our ankle arthritis exercises guide for a full routine. Can NHS podiatry help with foot arthritis? Yes. Ask your GP for a podiatry referral, or self-refer where your area allows it. Podiatrists assess biomechanics, advise on footwear and can prescribe custom orthotics that redistribute pressure away from painful joints. When should I see a GP about foot or ankle pain? Book an appointment if pain lasts more than a few weeks, limits walking, comes with warm swelling or deformity, or follows an old fracture. Seek urgent care for a hot, red, swollen joint with fever — that can be infection or acute crystal arthritis. Blog & Stories

/exercises/swimming-for-ankle-arthritis:
Swimming • Ankle Arthritis

Swimming is one of the most recommended activities for managing ankle arthritis. It helps reduce stiffness, strengthen the muscles around the ankle joint, and improve your overall mobility — all with minimal joint impact. This guide provides step-by-step exercises, benefits, and safety considerations specifically for ankle arthritis, based on UK physiotherapy guidelines.

Benefits of Swimming for Ankle Arthritis

  • Low-impact activity — water supports body weight
  • Improves cardiovascular fitness
  • Increases range of motion
  • Reduces stiffness and swelling
  • Strengthens muscles around joints

Recommended Ankle Exercises

1. Ankle Circles in Water

10 each direction

Hold pool edge, rotate each ankle slowly in water.

2. Toe Raises in Water

3 × 10

Stand in shallow water, rise onto toes, lower slowly.

3. Kick Board Kicks

5 minutes

Hold kickboard, flutter kick gently to mobilise ankles.

Safety Tips

  • Start with just 10-15 minutes and build up gradually
  • Warm water pools (28-32°C) are ideal for arthritic joints
  • Avoid butterfly stroke — it's too demanding on most joints
  • Wear aqua shoes for grip on pool sides

When to Avoid Swimming

  • During an active flare — rest and let it settle first
  • If you have open wounds or skin infections
  • If chlorine irritates your skin significantly

Printable companion sheets

Choose a one-page A4 sheet. Fill it in by hand and share only what you want with your healthcare team. The QR code and short link reopen this toolkit, not your completed notes.

  • GP appointment symptom and medication tracker (PDF)
  • Flare-up daily log (PDF)

Keep completed sheets somewhere private. Optional identifying details are for your own use. You do not need to sign in or upload anything. Updated resource guidance and new printables: separate clinical review pending.

When to get urgent help

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if a joint is swollen and feels hot, or joint pain comes with feeling unwell, a high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery.

Go to A&E or call 999 if you cannot walk or put weight on a joint, or have very bad joint pain after a fall or injury. Severe or worsening weakness or numbness in both legs, numbness around your genitals or bottom, or new bladder or bowel control problems also need emergency assessment.

If you are unsure, contact NHS 111. Do not wait to complete a tracker before seeking help.
